newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India state seeks business beyond pleasure.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India state seeks business beyond pleasure.

text.p: Palaces, maharajas, camels and sand dunes are proud symbols of Rajasthan, India's desert state, which attracts several thousands of tourists each year.
But officials in the northwestern state had never bargained that its image as a tourist paradise would stand in the way of its quest to attract investments.

They are now fighting hard to tell potential investors that the state is as rich in minerals as in minstrels, has electric power to match magnetic maharajas and offers a warm welcome to businessmen who need not necessarily be on holiday.

"Whenever we talk of investments, there is a faraway look in the businessman's eyes," Arvind Mayaram, the state's Commissioner, Investments, told Reuters. "There is a tremendous hiatus (difference) between reality and perception."

Mayaram cites facts he believes should wake up businessmen, as Rajasthan joins a host of Indian states to woo private investments in a market which has become highly competitive since India launched far-reaching economic reforms in 1991.
Rajasthan has the second largest deposit of non-ferrous metals in India. It produces 90 percent of India's gypsym, has high-grade limestone for steel melting and clays for ceramic.

State officials are reminding businessmen that there are granite, sandstone and slate deposits to fund a booming construction industry. They point to a rich stock of marble in the state, whose border is only 20 km (12 miles) away from the famed Mogul mausoleum in Agra, the Taj Mahal.
As the producer of almost all of India's copper, Rajasthan has the right base for metal works, state officials say.

During their colonial rule, British administrators built railways to criss-cross India, but could not do enough in Rajasthan, whose kings did not relish railways. This left a huge stock of mineral wealth unexploited, Mayaram said.

Officials' view that their state was a haven for investment suffered a jolt this year when South Korean car-maker Hyundai chose the southern state of Tamil Nadu to set up a new Indian plant, in preference over landlocked Rajasthan.
State officials say they lost the race as Rajasthan did not have a port, but add that all is not lost since it is still strategically located for business.

The highway that links India's financial centre, Bombay, with national capital New Delhi, runs across Rajasthan and passes through Gujarat, the coastal western state which has the highest growth rate in the country.

To the north of Rajasthan are the agricutlurally prosperous states of Haryana and Punjab, which offer high potential as markets for textiles, automobiles and goods like refrigerators and washing machines. "We are giving access to major markets in the country, not just one," Mayaram said.

Rajasthan is now trying to add value to its attractions by generating more electricity. At the time of independence in 1947, the state could produce only three megawatts of power. In 1996, the capacity stands at 3,600 megawatts.
The state expects to add another 4,000 megawatts by 2002, and is courting private firms to produce power.

Rajasthan is also on its way to building a dry port and an international air cargo airport at Jaipur, the state capital, to strengthen its infrastructure and make up for the disadvantage of not having a sea port.

The state is the traditional home of the rich Marwaris, a community which leads investors all over India, and officials hope that more Marwaris would come back home to an all-new Rajasthan, and would be accompanied by other investors from India and abroad.
"We have bombarded the investment system," Mayaram said. "Now we have to go for the kill."
